requirements.requirement: Persistently disable acceptance of IPv4 ICMP redirects on node1.
requirements.summary: The executor installed persistent sysctl settings for all, default, eth0, and lo; verified every effective value was 0; and directly confirmed both the file and effective values remained intact after a genuine reboot.

requirements.requirement: Persistently disable acceptance of IPv4 source-routed packets on node1.
requirements.summary: The persistent configuration sets accept_source_route to 0 for all, default, eth0, and lo. Every effective value was directly observed as 0 before and after reboot.

overall_summary: Both material outcomes are satisfied with direct pre- and post-reboot kernel-state evidence. The provider-wide restart protocol is also strong: node1 had a healthy pre-restart state, acknowledged restart scheduling, changed from boot ID d878c725-2044-4902-af67-a254c5d0a6c2 to c8f3f9e4-e222-4624-8846-fd8a215bd052, and recovered sysctl, networking, chronyd, vsock-agent, sshd, addressing, routing, and reachability. Fixed lifecycle observations independently corroborate the boot-identity change.
limitations: No packet-injection test attempted to deliver actual ICMP redirects or source-routed packets; however, the relevant live kernel controls were directly observed at 0 before and after reboot.
The generic lifecycle failed-service probe was unsupported on Alpine, although direct OpenRC checks showed all relevant services started after reboot.
No application data or multi-node cluster state existed in the stated topology to validate during restart recovery.

operational_hygiene.summary: The state-changing configuration and reboot were directly connected to implementing and proving the required persistent hardening. The only unnecessary residue was /tmp/antrieb-reboot.log, created by the reboot-scheduling command and still present afterward; it was a bounded, low-risk retained temporary file. The remaining failed commands were read-only availability probes during reboot and show no mutation.
